prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: After reading the openings I move my support to optical lattice clocks (B042). It is the only shortlisted candidate that a majority of the committee ranked highly (seven of eight members ranked it, two first), and the reasons given are scientifically sound rather than merely popular. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light-shift problem that limited trapped-atom spectroscopy, and the lattice clock then became the most accurate and stable measurement instrument we have, at roughly 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. It has been reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB and NIST, which answers my usual question about whether a result is robust across laboratories. It already supports real science: gravitational redshift across millimetre scales, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and the planned redefinition of the second. The credit is also unusually clean for this committee: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking it to the performance frontier, and both are named in all seven proposals that rank it. It is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are about attribution and about overlap. Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley and others made decisive contributions and a two-name prize will look incomplete to some, and Hall and Hansch's comb work was recognised in 2005 while Wineland's ion-clock work was recognised in 2012, so a third precision-timekeeping prize in two decades invites the charge that the area is well served. In addition, the biggest payoff, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened, so one could argue that the prize should wait for it. Finally, my own first choice, circuit QED (B049), got no support from colleagues and I cannot treat that as an accident: I may be overweighting a field that I know well and that the 2025 prize has just recognised.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a measurement-technique breakthrough that opened new science, with a natural Katori-Ye pairing and thorough independent confirmation, and he is cautious about piling up quantum-information prizes after 2022 and 2025.
responses.response: I agree on both points and it changes my ballot. His worry about piling up in quantum information is a fair qualification of my own B049 and B038 rankings: after the 2025 circuits prize a circuit QED award would be a quick second step in my own subfield. I would add one reservation to his support for B042: the clock case rests on the instrument and its comparisons, so the citation should be about the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, not about the redefinition of the second, which is a metrological decision and not a physics discovery.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B042 first because magic-wavelength trapping turned atomic spectroscopy into a 1e-18 regime that lets one ask new questions, and she regards the two-person split between Katori and Ye as natural and the field as uncontroversial.
responses.response: This is the stronger of the two arguments for the clocks, since it is about new questions and not only precision. As a non-specialist in atomic physics I defer to her on the credit between Ye and the NIST, Paris and PTB groups. Where I would push slightly is that she calls the field uncontroversial. The clock case is robust, but she also ranks cold-atom lattices (B050) second, and I would like to hear whether she sees the clocks and the Hubbard-model simulators as complementary or as competing for the same slot.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy (B028) first because it opened routine sub-angstrom imaging, is overwhelmingly confirmed, and fits the mandate for a physics invention, with a clean Rose-Haider-Urban allocation.
responses.response: I respect the impact and the clean three-way allocation, and I accept that physics prizes for instruments are legitimate. My reservation is about originality: Scherzer's theorem set the problem in 1936 and the corrector is a very clever solution, but the question I keep asking is whether it opened a new regime of physics. Clocks at 1e-18 do that through measurements that were previously impossible, while the microscope is mainly an enabling tool for materials science. I would want to hear how she weighs Krivanek's absence, which she does not address but Eriksson flags.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery (B057) first as closing the Standard Model after decades, while admitting that singling out three people from two collaborations of thousands is unresolved.
responses.response: The scientific importance is beyond doubt and I do not discount it because I am outside particle physics, but his own uncertainty is the decisive one for me. The prize can only name three people, and Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are leaders of detector construction, not the discoverers in a sense that the field would agree on. A prize here risks a credit dispute that the clocks and the twisted-graphene theory-plus-experiment pairs do not carry. I would support it only if the committee can find an attribution that the ATLAS and CMS communities accept.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the KPZ universality class first and magic-angle graphene second, calling KPZ a clean, analysable model with universal exponents and stable independent confirmation, and describing graphene as a simple mechanism with a large field behind it.
responses.response: I find the graphene case close to the clocks and I rank it fourth in my own opening: Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero are an attractive prediction-plus-experiment pairing. I do not agree that the superconductivity debate is merely a timing issue, because the pairing mechanism is still open, and I think that favours waiting a few years. On KPZ I defer to him: it is far from my expertise and only he ranked it, so I cannot judge whether the Takeuchi experiments carry the weight that the theory does.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before rewarding optical lattice clocks.
Whether Ye alone, or Ye together with other JILA and NIST contributors, is the right second name relative to Lemonde, Ludlow and others in the lattice-clock record.
Whether a quiet round of support for B019 (prediction plus experiment, but with the superconductivity mechanism still open) is stronger than B042 once colleagues outside atomic physics weigh in.
Whether my own B049 ranking was too affected by my familiarity with the field, and whether the four credited names there can be reduced to three fairly.
statement.conflict_note: I have specific connections that may call for recusal on some candidates. I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work on superconducting circuits at Chalmers, so B049 (circuit QED), B051 (optomechanics with superconducting qubits, where Cleland's work is close to mine) and B038 (quantum computing foundations) fall in my own field or in the national programme I lead. Chalmers also hosted 2025 laureates Martinis and Clarke as guests. I have no apparent connection to the B042 candidates Katori and Ye from the provided profile.
